depth_justification: The copilot references SkinTrack-specific facts (the self-chosen 20% area-change threshold, mole photos with location/date as GDPR Art. 9 data, uncalibrated photo variability), but it cycles repetitively around 2-3 themes and entirely misses the central risk the developer flagged twice: whether the 'see a dermatologist' nudge makes this an EU MDR medical device (no Rule 11 / intended-purpose analysis). The final report even cites the EU AI Act Art. 16 despite the app explicitly having 'No AI', showing the analysis was not grounded in this app's actual facts.
actionability_justification: Mitigations stay directional ('Conduct a clinical validation study', 'Perform a DPIA under Article 35', 'Add a prominent disclaimer') with a couple of standards references (ISO 82304-2, GDPR Art. 9/35) but no concrete implementation recipes (no disclaimer wording, no consent-UI design, no MDR classification steps), and the in-conversation turns were almost all info-gathering questions offering the developer nothing to implement.
salient_examples: Conduct a clinical validation study in line with ISO 82304-2 to establish evidence-based thresholds and publish results.
violating the EU AI Act’s transparency and safety requirements [Article 16(1)]
Mitigation: Add a prominent disclaimer stating that the app is not a medical assessment and that no alerts do not imply stability, in line with Article 9 of GDPR for health data.
How does SkinTrack address the risk of users misinterpreting the absence of alerts as an indication that their moles are stable...
